description: Sitaara is on a mission to make complex observations of our planet understandable to everyone. We turn hard-to-read scientific data into clear, honest and engaging experiences, labelling what is real and what is illustrative and treating every interpretation as a hypothesis. Our vision is a future where anyone, from a student to a community decision-maker, can explore the rhythms of the Earth through approachable, open tools, with careful storytelling and rigorous science working together.
summary:
FASAL (Urdu: فصل, "crop season") is an open-source interactive web app that turns radar backscatter time series into the seasonal rhythm of farmland on the Indus plains. It follows three sites in Pakistan: the Central Punjab rice-wheat belt, Larkana and Mohenjo-daro, and Tharparkar. A time scrubber moves a radar frame, a backscatter chart and a generated tone together, while cultural dates such as Baisakhi, regional folk tales and a historical-map swipe add local context. Each site ends in a printable one-page Field Record.

The app answers the challenge by making L-band SAR, which sees through monsoon cloud day and night, understandable to scientists, educators and the public. Every reading is worded as a hypothesis ("consistent with flooded paddy"), never as ground truth, and cropping intensity is estimated only when at least 20 acquisitions span a full year. A Python pipeline that searches ASF for NISAR GCOV data and extracts per-field backscatter is included.

Punjab uses limited NISAR acquisitions from 2025 to 2026; the other sites are clearly labelled illustrative demo data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

FASAL turns radar backscatter time series into an interactive "rhythm of the land" for three sites in Pakistan: the Central Punjab rice-wheat belt (the hero site), Larkana and Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, and Tharparkar, a rain-fed desert district. Users move through time with a brass-dial scrubber; the radar frame, a backscatter chart and a generated tone change together. Cultural dates (such as Baisakhi) and detected radar signals appear as markers on the same timeline. Each site also has a folk tale retold in our own words, a before/after swipe against a public-domain historical map (when a verified map is added), and a printable one-page Field Record.

HOW IT WORKS

An offline Python pipeline searches the ASF archive for NISAR GCOV granules, reads backscatter from the HDF5 files, and for each sample field takes the mean in linear power before converting to decibels. The site series is the median across fields with an interquartile band. A simple smoothing step feeds transparent rules that produce hints worded as hypotheses: sustained low backscatter in the monsoon window is consistent with standing water, a later rise with canopy growth, and an abrupt fall after a peak with harvest or clearing. Cropping intensity is estimated only if at least 20 acquisitions span at least 365 days; otherwise the app displays "Insufficient dates for cropping-intensity estimate." The app also shows how many acquisitions are available and discusses limits: revisit gaps, speckle, incidence-angle and soil-moisture effects, no ground truth, and small sample polygons.

DATA STATUS

Punjab uses limited NISAR acquisitions from 2025 to 2026. Larkana and Tharparkar remain labelled illustrative demo data. The banner, sensor labels and acquisition counts show which is which.

INTENDED IMPACT

FASAL is a prototype for how repeat L-band observations could give smallholder communities, extension services and educators an independent record of when fields are flooded, growing or cleared, especially where cloud blocks optical satellites. This is a future direction, not a validated service, and we make no yield or food-security claims.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, d3-geo, HTML canvas and SVG, Framer Motion, Recharts, Zustand and the Web Audio API for the app; Python, asf_search, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, pandas and Pillow for the pipeline. Open source (MIT), deployed from GitHub.

CREATIVITY

An astro-cartographic "antique observatory" interface drawn entirely in code: engraved globe, armillary rings, radar sweep, parchment surfaces and brass instruments. The backscatter becomes sound ("Earth's Choir"): lower backscatter gives a lower, darker tone and higher gives a brighter one, with a visible text equivalent. There are no external images or audio.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty (real and demo data are labelled everywhere), accessibility (keyboard operation, ARIA labels, reduced-motion support, contrast), local context (Urdu text, regional stories, cultural dates, each with a source note), and limits.

AI ASSISTANCE

This project was developed with assistance from Claude (Anthropic) for ideation, research, data-analysis design, and drafting and debugging code and text, including the web app, the Python pipeline and the synthetic demo-data generator. No image- or audio-generation tools were used, and no NASA logos or branding appear.
